findings.headline: 2026/27 budget allocates only £6m to rebuild reserves described as urgently needed
findings.detail: Recognizing critically low reserves, the 2026/27 budget has allocated £6m to replenish the MTFS reserve. The statement explicitly describes this as an 'urgent need' to rebuild reserves 'both immediately and incrementally over the MTFS period' to restore 'safer and more sustainable level of financial protection'.
findings.matters: £6m allocation against 'critically low' reserves over a multi-year period confirms severe reserve depletion and indicates incremental recovery will take years, leaving the council at heightened risk in the interim
findings.figures: £6m allocated to MTFS Reserve in 2026/27 budget; described as starting a process over MTFS period
findings.quote: There is an urgent need to rebuild reserves, both immediately and incrementally over the MTFS period, to restore a safer and more sustainable level of financial protection. The Budget for 2026/27 starts the process of addressing this by allocating £6 million to replenish the MTFS Reserve.

findings.paper_title: 9.1 2026 Annual Governance Statement - working draft for Gov Cttee - App 1
findings.headline: New escalation procedure for audit actions indicates previous non-delivery of recommendations
findings.detail: A new escalation procedure has been introduced during 2026/27 to ensure robust monitoring of audit action delivery. Where audit actions fall overdue, they will be escalated and action holders can be requested to appear before Governance Committee. This implies previous audit actions were not being completed on time.
findings.matters: Audit actions are improvements to control environment weaknesses; failure to implement them on schedule indicates management capacity issues or governance culture challenges in addressing control gaps
findings.figures: Quarterly reporting of outstanding audit actions introduced; escalation to Governance Committee for significantly overdue items
findings.quote: A new escalation procedure has been introduced during 2026/27 to ensure robust monitoring of the delivery of audit actions and recommendations. A quarterly report on outstanding audit actions is presented by the Assistant Director of Finance to the Executive Management Team, alongside the existing reporting to Risk Management Group. If audit actions fall overdue, this will provide the initial step for escalation.

findings.paper_title: 9.1 2026 Annual Governance Statement - working draft for Gov Cttee - App 1
findings.headline: Internal Audit opinion is Reasonable Assurance with acknowledged weaknesses rather than Substantial Assurance
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit opinion for 2025/26 was Reasonable Assurance, the second highest on a four-point scale. While the council states this 'does not suggest that the council is carrying unacceptable levels of risk', it explicitly identifies 'weaknesses and improvement opportunities' in the governance and control framework.
findings.matters: Audit opinion below Substantial Assurance indicates material weaknesses in internal controls and governance that could affect financial reporting reliability and service delivery effectiveness
findings.figures: Reasonable Assurance opinion on four-point scale (No Assurance to Substantial Assurance)
findings.quote: The overall opinion of the Head of Internal Audit on the framework of governance, risk management and control operating at the Council for 2025/26 was that it provides 'reasonable assurance'. Whilst the Reasonable Assurance opinion suggests that there are weaknesses and improvement opportunities, it does not suggest that the council is carrying unacceptable levels of risk

findings.paper_title: 9.1 2026 Annual Governance Statement - working draft for Gov Cttee - App 1
findings.headline: Children's social care experiencing sustained demand and cost crisis with 431 children in care and volatile placements
findings.detail: The council continues to experience significant budget pressures driven by increasing numbers of children in care requiring high-cost placements. Numbers have fluctuated between 410-450 over the last six months as at June 2026. This is the main driver of financial pressures and is described as 'particularly acute'.
findings.matters: Children's social care is a statutory service where underfunding creates safeguarding risks and failure to meet demand. High-cost placement inflation is the primary budget pressure and transformation activity shows no resolution in sight
findings.figures: 431 children in care as at 22 June 2026; numbers fluctuating between 410-450 across last 6 months; £3m capital investment plus £2m transformational investment allocated
findings.quote: The outturn position for 2025/26 was a pressure of £2.412m...The position continues to be driven by increasing pressures within Children's Social Care, with the numbers of children in high-cost placements continuing to rise. This pressure, along with broader service demands...have led to a substantial reduction in reserves, now at critically low levels.

findings.headline: Council depends on £18.4m exceptional financial support from government to balance 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: The council has secured in-principle agreement for £18.4m in exceptional financial support to bridge a projected 2026/27 budget gap. findings.figures: £18.4m exceptional financial support required for 2026/27
findings.quote: With limited scope for future savings, the Authority has secured in principle agreement from Government for exceptional financial support (EFS). The scheme supports Authority's facing acute financial challenges in bridging short-term budget gaps, where a path to sustainability exists. The Authority has planned to utilise £18.4m of EFS to support the balancing of its 2026/27 Budget

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Outturn Cabinet Report - Cabinet (final)
findings.headline: Council debt increased to £247.069m from £225.864m in Q3; now in overborrowing position of £9.685m against Capital Financing Requirement
findings.detail: Debt rose by £21.2m in final quarter (Q4) due to £27.5m new PWLB loans and £2.5m local authority loan, less repayment instalments. The council's Capital Financing Requirement is £289.205m (adjusted to £237.384m for PFI/lease liabilities), but actual borrowing is £247.069m, creating an overborrowing position of £9.685m. This breaches the CFR but remains within the authorised operational limit. The overborrowing is primarily attributable to the DSG deficit (£21.083m), which should reverse once the government's High Needs Stability Grant is received (pending SEND reform plan approval).
findings.matters: An overborrowing position is technically a prudential code breach (even if within authorised limits) and creates contingent refinancing risk if the DSG grant does not materialise as expected. The council has deliberately borrowed more than its CFR to manage the DSG deficit impact.
findings.figures: Total debt £247.069m (up from £225.864m in Q3); CFR £289.205m (adjusted £237.384m); overborrowing £9.685m; new PWLB loans £27.5m; local authority loan £2.5m; DSG deficit £21.083m
findings.quote: When this is compared to the Council's borrowing of £247.069 million this results in an overborrowing position of £9.685 million. The main driver of this over borrowed position is the DSG deficit of £21.083 million referenced within this report. It is anticipated that once the local SEND reform plan is secured, c£18.975 million of our forecast 2025/26-year end deficit should be addressed via the High Needs Stability Grant reversing this over borrowed position.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Outturn Cabinet Report - Cabinet (final)
findings.headline: Council approved £3.5m additional capital borrowing for ERP system replacement with current system end-of-life by 30 September 2027
findings.detail: The council's current Enterprise Resource Planning system (supporting HR, finance, payroll, procurement) expires on 30 September 2027 and cannot be extended. A comprehensive options appraisal identified replacement as unavoidable and time-critical. The preferred solution (Option 3) involves £3.5 million capital investment funded via borrowing, with implementation by the supplier's in-house team (claimed 95% on-time, on-budget delivery track record). Revenue costs will be met from existing transformation budgets.
findings.matters: An aging, non-extensible critical system creates binary risk: borrow now and replace on schedule, or face operational failure post-September 2027. A lender needs assurance that implementation is realistic; the council rejected Option 2 partly due to third-party implementation partner risk.
findings.figures: £3.5m capital investment; 15-year financing period; system end-of-life 30 September 2027; Option 3 chosen over Option 1 (£2.8m, current supplier) and Option 2 (£3.25m, third-party implementation risk)
findings.quote: The Council is required to replace its existing Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) system, which supports critical financial, human resources, payroll and procurement functions, ahead of the expiry of the current contract on 30 September 2027. This report therefore seeks approval for an additional £3.5m of capital investment, funded through borrowing, to support the implementation of a new ERP system.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Outturn Cabinet Report - Cabinet (final)
findings.headline: Adult social care overspent by £1.784m; winter pressures and hospital discharge delays driving residential placement demand
findings.detail: Adult and Community Services overspent by £1.784 million, primarily due to increased demand for residential care. The paper specifically cites impact of 2025 winter pressures and hospital discharge arrangements, noting that some patients placed in short-term residential beds became permanent residents. Actions taken include changes to hospital discharge pathways and investment in hospital social work resource, and the trend has "levelled out".
findings.matters: Adult social care demand is structural and will intensify with demographic change. An overspend driven by hospital discharge suggests systemic rather than temporary pressures, and control measures appear reactive rather than preventive.
findings.figures: £1.784m overspend in Adult and Community Services
findings.quote: The Directorate have incurred an overspend of £1.784 million versus budget. The majority of the overspend related to increased demand for residential care, with the impact of the 2025 winter pressures still impacting as well as hospitals in crisis exasperating volume pressures nationally as well as here in Redcar and Cleveland.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Outturn Cabinet Report - Cabinet (final)
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit increased £8.628m to cumulative £21.083m; statutory override expires 2028 with no funded solution yet confirmed
findings.detail: The DSG High Needs Block deficit grew significantly from £12.455m to £21.083m. The council operates under a statutory override that isolates this from usable reserves, but that override expires 31 March 2028. Government has committed to resolving 90% of deficits accrued to end-2025/26 via a High Needs Stability Grant (subject to council approval of a local SEND reform plan), but the remaining 10% and any post-2028 deficits have no confirmed funding source.
findings.matters: Although currently ring-fenced by statute, this deficit will crystallise as a real financial liability post-2028 unless government assumptions about demand change dramatically. The council cannot control SEND placement demand directly, creating medium-term budget risk.
findings.figures: 2024/25 DSG deficit £12.455m; 2025/26 deficit increase £8.628m; end-of-year deficit £21.083m; government to resolve ~£18.975m (90%) via Stability Grant if SEND reform plan approved; statutory override expires 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The DSG deficit has increased by a further £8.628 million in 2025/26 to an overall deficit of £21.083 million as at 31 March 2026. The increasing pressure in DSG, and in particular the High Needs Block, is because alongside social care, education services are experiencing an increase in more complex placements requiring a place in special schools.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Outturn Cabinet Report - Cabinet (final)
findings.headline: Usable reserves fell 10% in year: from £17.628m to £15.997m, with MTFS Reserve drawn down £1.309m despite approved top-up
findings.detail: The council drew down £1.309 million from the Medium-Term Financial Strategy Reserve during 2025/26 to fund the overspend position, despite an approved £0.936 million top-up in the February 2025 budget. Overall reserves declined by approximately 10% across the year. The council held back some mitigating measures by using in-year underspends and release of other reserves, but the underlying trajectory is negative.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce financial flexibility and increase vulnerability to future shocks. A 10% annual drawdown at this scale is unsustainable and signals the council is consuming rather than building resilience.
findings.figures: Opening reserves £17.628m; closing reserves £15.997m; MTFS Reserve drawdown £1.309m; approved top-up £0.936m; total year reduction £1.631m (10%)
findings.quote: The approved 2025/26 Budget included a £0.936 million top-up to the MTFS Reserve. However, a combination of factors, such as delays in delivering all planned transformation savings and the continuing in-year pressures contributing to the 2025/26 overspend of £2.412 million, mean that the Council has needed to draw down £1.309 million of the MTFS Reserve during 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Outturn Cabinet Report - Cabinet (final)
findings.headline: Transformation Programme delivered only 52% of planned £8.848m savings; £4.208m of savings unachieved
findings.detail: The council achieved £4.640 million of planned transformation savings but missed £4.208 million (48%). The majority of unachieved balance relates to asset sales (£2.332 million shortfall) and delays in developing in-house children's care placements (£1.780 million of £2.918 million saving unachieved). Both initiatives remain ongoing and are expected to deliver in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Failed transformation programmes signal operational execution risk and can cascade into future budget failures if assumed savings do not materialise. Asset sale delays in particular can reflect either market conditions or organisational capability constraints.
findings.figures: £8.848m planned savings; £4.640m achieved (52%); £4.208m not achieved (48%); asset sales shortfall £2.332m; children's placements in-house development shortfall £1.780m
findings.quote: The Transformation Programme sought to deliver planned savings of £8.848 million in 2025/26. In summary £4.640 million of these savings have been classified as being achieved (52%) and £4.208 million (48%) were not achieved. The majority of the unachieved balance relates to the sale of fixed assets and savings from the development of in-house children's care placements.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Outturn Cabinet Report - Cabinet (final)
findings.headline: Collection Fund deteriorated sharply in Q4: council tax moved from £0.641m surplus to £1.164m deficit; business rates from £0.776m surplus to £2.232m deficit
findings.detail: Council tax collection fund shifted £1.805 million from Q3 position due to increased discounts and exemptions plus higher bad debt provisions. Business rates swung £1.552 million due to Teesworks income delays, a large hereditament appeal success, and increased appeals provisions in the final quarter. The council's retained share is £0.967m (council tax) and £1.094m (business rates), totalling £2.061m of deficits to be managed.
findings.matters: A deteriorating collection fund signals either structural challenges in the tax base or forecast accuracy issues, both material to lender confidence. The sharp Q4 movement suggests risk management gaps and the impact feeds directly into 2027/28 budget planning.
findings.figures: Council tax: £1.164m deficit (council share £0.967m); business rates: £2.232m deficit (council share £1.094m); council tax Q3-to-outturn swing £1.805m; business rates swing £1.552m
findings.quote: For council tax, the total year-end deficit as referenced in Appendix 1 is £1.164 million (compared to a surplus of £0.641 million in Quarter 3). The Council retains an 83% share of this deficit, which equates to £0.967million. This worsened year-end position has arisen due an increase in discounts and exemptions which has lowered the overall income into the Collection Fund.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Outturn Cabinet Report - Cabinet (final)
findings.headline: Children's Services overspend of £7.132m driven by high-cost residential placements hitting £8.452m over budget
findings.detail: Children in care placement costs totalled £43.779 million against a budget expectation, with residential and supported accommodation placements alone £7.172 million over budget. The council placed an average of 96.6 children in these high-cost settings, rising to 104 by end of March 2026. Each placement costs approximately £0.322 million annually. The overspend reflects both rising numbers and increasing complexity of children's needs.
findings.matters: A lender assessing financial sustainability needs to understand whether this is a one-off or structural demand pressure; children's services is typically the most volatile budget and this overspend consumed most of the year's total variance.
findings.figures: £43.779 million actual vs budget; £8.452 million overspend; £7.172 million on residential/supported accommodation alone; average 96.6 children, peak 104; £0.322 million per placement per annum
findings.quote: Children in our care placement costs were £43.779 million, which was £8.452 million higher than budget (£7.438 million higher at Q3). The worsening position relates to the increased number and cost of children in high-cost placements, specifically residential and supported accommodation, which was £7.172 million (£6.060 million at Q3).

findings.paper_title: Finance report childrens summary Outturn 2025 2026
findings.headline: A £2.918m transformation savings target for in-borough children's placements is only 44% delivered, with more than half still outstanding
findings.detail: The council targeted £2.918m in savings from developing more in-borough placements for children in care. By year-end, only £1.291m (44%) was achieved, with £1.627m (56%) carried forward. The council attributes this to Ofsted approval delays rather than plan failure, but the shortfall remains.
findings.matters: A lender reviewing deficit management needs to know whether savings plans are on track. This plan is significantly behind. If not recovered in 2026/27, it signals the council's savings forecast was too optimistic.
findings.figures: £2.918m target; £1.291m (44%) achieved; £1.627m (56%) unachieved as at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: There was a target for 2025/26 of £2.918m. As at 31 March 2026, £1.291m (44%) had been achieved with £1.627m (56%) still to achieve.

findings.paper_title: Finance report childrens summary Outturn 2025 2026
findings.headline: Children's social work recruitment remains unresolved, forcing continued reliance on agency workers costing £0.990m despite falling from the prior year
findings.detail: The council holds social work vacancies as a cost control, creating £1.119m in staffing underspend. However, this forces use of agency workers at £0.990m. Agency costs have fallen from £1.446m in 2024/25, suggesting some improvement, but the council still cannot recruit to its permanent establishment.
findings.matters: Persistent recruitment failure in a critical service is a risk indicator. The council is managing cost by understaffing and using agency workers, which is neither sustainable nor cost-effective long-term.
findings.figures: £0.990m agency spend in 2025/26; £1.446m in 2024/25 (32% reduction); £1.119m underspend from staffing vacancies
findings.quote: Staffing costs across all social worker areas were £0.129m lower than budget. There were total staffing savings of £1.119m, created from the holding of vacancies. This represents the difficulties of recruiting still being experienced in the market.

findings.paper_title: Finance report childrens summary Outturn 2025 2026
findings.headline: Independent and Non-Maintained Special Schools placements have more than doubled in four years, driving a £5.073m overspend with no corresponding budget increase
findings.detail: INMSS placements grew from 68 children in 2020/21 to 165 in 2025/26 (142.7% increase), while average cost per place rose 31.2% from £0.050m to £0.066m. The budget did not grow in line with this demand; despite a £2.929m overspend in 2024/25, it remained largely unchanged for 2025/26.
findings.matters: This is a sustained, accelerating demand that the council cannot fund. It is the largest single pressure in the High Needs Block and will recur annually without external intervention or funding reform.
findings.figures: 165 children vs 68 in 2020/21 (142.7% increase); average cost £0.066m in 2025/26 vs £0.050m in 2020/21 (31.2% increase); £5.073m overspend
findings.quote: The number of children within these placements has increased over the same period from 68 to 165 which is an increase of 142.7%.

findings.paper_title: Finance report childrens summary Outturn 2025 2026
findings.headline: DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) deficit has accumulated to £21.083m and is ring-fenced, requiring it to be carried forward indefinitely
findings.detail: The High Needs Block overspent by £8.628m in 2025/26, adding to a £12.455m prior-year carry-forward. The total £21.083m deficit must be carried forward because DSG is ring-fenced. The council's SEND Reform Plan could reduce this by £18.975m (90% reduction) if approved, but depends on a Schools White Paper not yet released and expires as a reserve override on 31 March 2028.
findings.matters: An accumulated £21m liability is material. It signals the High Needs Block is fundamentally under-resourced. The council's solution depends on external approval and has an expiry date, creating an uncertain tail risk.
findings.figures: £21.083m total DSG deficit (£12.455m prior year + £8.628m 2025/26); £18.975m expected reduction from reform plan if approved; override expires 31 March 2028
findings.quote: DSG is a ring-fenced grant and as such this year-end deficit balance is carried forward to the next financial year. The balance from the previous year end is £12.455m creating a total deficit at the end of 25/26 of £21.083m.

findings.paper_title: Finance report childrens summary Outturn 2025 2026
findings.headline: Children's placement costs overran by £8.452m, driven by 27 more children in care and 24 more high-cost residential placements than budgeted
findings.detail: The council budgeted for 376 children in care but had an average of 403. High-cost residential placements rose from 73 budgeted to 97 actual, at an average cost of £0.322m per child. The overspend worsened by £1.016m in Q4 alone, signalling an unresolved structural pressure.
findings.matters: A lender must know whether this is a one-off or a structural gap in budget forecasting. These are uncontrollable demand drivers that repeat annually and erode council reserves.
findings.figures: 403 children vs 376 budgeted; 97 residential placements vs 73 budgeted; £0.322m average cost per residential place; £8.452m total overspend; £1.016m worsening in Q4
findings.quote: The Budget for 2025/26 was built on the Council having an average of 376 children in its care over the financial year. The actual average was significantly higher with 403 children in our care.

findings.paper_title: RTPHA Financial Position 2025-26 Unaudited accounts report final
findings.headline: Veterinary and staff costs are rising due to demand from increased animal disease checks, showing inflation in a core service area.
findings.detail: Staff costs overran by £12,477 due to 'additional overtime to support meeting demand of BTOM and supplement to two employees'. Other operating costs exceeded budget by £24,791 due to 'additional veterinary service provision to cover increase in checks following outbreaks of animal related diseases in the EU and increased computer licence costs (£6k)'.
findings.matters: If disease prevalence increases further, the Authority has limited headroom to absorb costs, creating risk of budget pressure or funding calls on member councils including Redcar and Cleveland.
findings.figures: Staff costs overspend £12,477; other operating costs overspend £24,791; total expenditure variance £37,268
findings.quote: Other Operating Costs - overspend of £24,791– this is demand driven, including additional veterinary service provision to cover increase in checks following outbreaks of animal related diseases in the EU and increased computer licence costs (£6k).

findings.paper_title: RTPHA Financial Position 2025-26 Unaudited accounts report final
findings.headline: Management is building reserves specifically to hedge against EU trade deal impacts and 2027 legislative changes, signalling concern about future financial stability.
findings.detail: The Authority is requesting approval to transfer a £128,543 underspend to reserves 'to help mitigate the continued risks associated with the transition to a Target Operating Model (TOM), expected future legislative changes (planned for 2027) any other unforeseen costs'. The report explicitly notes that clarity on the EU trade deal impact will be provided later, and reserves are being built to provide 'resilience versus potential adverse changes'.
findings.matters: This indicates management anticipates material adverse impacts from trade policy or legislative change, creating downside risk to the Authority's finances and to Redcar and Cleveland's own budget if costs or contributions must increase.
findings.figures: Reserves carried forward £511,986 (up from £380,414); underspend transfer £128,543; cash in hand £508,035
findings.quote: Approve the transfer of an underspend of £128,543 achieved in 2025/26, to reserves for carry-forward and use in 2026/27, to help mitigate the continued risks associated with the transition to a Target Operating Model (TOM), expected future legislative changes (planned for 2027) any other unforeseen costs.

findings.paper_title: RTPHA Financial Position 2025-26 Unaudited accounts report final
findings.headline: Nearly £160k of the income surplus came from animal health checks that were largely unknown and dependent on external EU disease events.
findings.detail: The Authority budgeted for £660,500 in income but received £825,440, creating a variance of £164,940. Of this, £159,916 came from 'additional product of animal origin income (£159,916 additional) which was largely unknown'. This income is tied to increased disease checks following EU animal outbreaks and is not a recurring revenue stream that can be relied upon.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director needs to assess whether funding is stable; income dependent on external disease prevalence could reverse, creating sudden budget pressure on Redcar and Cleveland, which contributes £81,978 to the Authority.
findings.figures: Income variance £164,940; animal-origin income £159,916; total income £825,440 vs budget £660,500
findings.quote: Income - £164,940 more than budget primarily as a result of additional product of animal origin income (£159,916 additional) which was largely unknown.

findings.paper_title: Budget Proposals 26-27 combined
findings.headline: Transformation savings capacity severely constrained with only £7.2 million identified across entire five-year medium-term financial strategy
findings.detail: Despite four years of delivering over £20 million in savings, the council has identified only £7.172 million in new savings across the entire medium-term financial strategy. The document explicitly states 'the scope for further efficiencies is constrained' and the savings programme has been 'deliberately targeted and proportionate' given previous extensive programmes. This limited savings capacity means the council has minimal ability to address unexpected cost pressures or demand spikes beyond what the budget already assumes.
findings.matters: When a council cannot find meaningful additional savings despite acute financial pressure, it signals that service cuts have reached their practical limit; any deterioration beyond budget assumptions must then be met through emergency borrowing or service reductions with adverse impacts.
findings.figures: Savings delivered in previous four years: over £20 million; new savings planned for MTFS period: £7.172 million (less than two years of current annual savings rate)
findings.quote: Given the Council's current financial position and the extensive savings delivered in recent years, the scope for further efficiencies is constrained and the savings programme has therefore been deliberately targeted and proportionate.

findings.paper_title: Budget Proposals 26-27 combined
findings.headline: Structural funding disadvantage of approximately £25 million over three years due to revised deprivation formula in finance settlement
findings.detail: Under the revised children's services funding formula, Redcar and Cleveland was downgraded from earlier proposals due to changes to deprivation measures. The council documents that authorities which benefited most from this change have average children in care rates ranked 130th nationally—less than one-third of Redcar and Cleveland's rate—yet receive significantly higher Core Spending Power increases (averaging 30.3% versus 14 percentage points lower for Redcar and Cleveland). This structural disadvantage is not a consequence of transformation success or inefficiency, but of the national funding formula parameters.
findings.matters: A structural underfunding of this magnitude indicates the council cannot resolve its children's services financial crisis through transformation or efficiency; it requires change to the national funding formula or ongoing supplementary government support, both of which are beyond the council's control.
findings.figures: Redcar and Cleveland funding formula ranking: 44th for assessed need (deterioration from earlier proposals); funding differential over settlement period: approximately £25 million; comparison authorities average CSP increase: 30.3% vs Redcar and Cleveland's 16.3%
findings.quote: For Redcar and Cleveland, each 1% of Core Spending Power equates to approximately £1.8 million, meaning this differential would equate to around £25 million of additional funding over the settlement period.

findings.paper_title: Budget Proposals 26-27 combined
findings.headline: Schools High Needs deficit of £20.2 million forecast by end of 2025/26 with resolution dependent on conditional government grant
findings.detail: The council's SEND deficit is forecast to reach £20.2 million by end of 2025/26. The government has announced a High Needs Stability Grant to resolve approximately 90% of accumulated deficits, which would address approximately £18 million of Redcar and Cleveland's deficit. However, this grant is conditional on Department for Education approval of a local SEND reform plan. The document notes 'further detail is awaited' in the Schools White Paper on how residual deficits will be addressed after the statutory override expires in March 2028, creating uncertainty about post-2028 liability.
findings.matters: A £20 million education deficit is a substantial contingent liability; while the government has signalled support, the relief is conditional (requiring DfE approval) and temporary (statutory override expires 2028), creating material future budget risk.
findings.figures: SEND deficit forecast for end of 25/26: £20.2 million; High Needs Stability Grant expected to resolve approximately £18 million if DfE approval of reform plan is secured; statutory override expires March 2028

findings.paper_title: Budget Proposals 26-27 combined

The council is attempting to manage demand through transformation activity and in-borough care market development, but acknowledges that 'further escalation can be slowed' only through successful delivery of these initiatives, indicating uncertainty about containment.

findings.matters: A widening budget gap combined with depleted reserves indicates financial deterioration between forecast and outcome; temporary borrowing schemes mask underlying deficits and create material refinancing risk when flexibilities expire.

findings.matters: Reserve depletion is the primary indicator of financial distress; a council with inadequate reserves cannot absorb unexpected cost spikes without emergency borrowing or service cuts, and faces significantly elevated refinancing risk.

The council should avoid asset sales that do not represent value for money and dispose of community heritage assets only where unavoidable.
findings.matters: This directive constrains the council's borrowing flexibility going forward. It signals the government's concern about debt sustainability and forces reliance on capital receipts—which may require asset disposals or create funding competition between services.

They reduce the council's ability to afford essential services and future capital investment. The fact that £17.372m of existing debt is allocated to this non-productive cost matters to creditors assessing debt serviceability.
findings.figures: £17.372 million net premium outstanding on 31 March 2026
findings.quote: Premiums and discounts incurred in the restructuring of the Lender Option – Borrower Option (LOBO) and market loans... The net premium outstanding on the 31 March 2026 is £17.372 million.

findings.paper_title: 8.1 Capital and Treasury Strategy 26-27 v2
findings.headline: External borrowing accelerating sharply: up £26.922m to £263.821m in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council's forecast external borrowing requirement is increasing by £26.922m in 2026/27 alone, on top of £20.554m in 2025/26. This acceleration reflects both the capital programme and the DSG deficit requiring debt finance. The council explicitly notes this is driven by 'the impact of the DSG deficit and the use of reserves to fund pressures in the revenue budget.'
findings.matters: Rapidly escalating borrowing, especially when driven by non-discretionary spend (DSG), signals weakening financial control. If capital borrowing is accelerating this fast, there is little room for the council to manage new pressures or invest in resilience without breaching debt limits.
findings.quote: The Council's level of external loans is anticipated to be £236.899 million at the end of 2025/26, an increase of £20.554 million on the previous year... due to funding the in-year capital investment programme less the in-year Minimum Revenue Payment, the impact of the DSG deficit and the use of reserves to fund pressures in the revenue budget.

findings.paper_title: 8.1 Capital and Treasury Strategy 26-27 v2
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £20m existing plus £8m additional in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council faces a growing DSG deficit, with £20m already accrued as of March 2026 and a further £8m anticipated during the coming financial year. This deficit is not part of the Capital Financing Requirement but represents real debt that impacts the council's liquidity and overall borrowing position. The council has been forced to borrow to cover this unfunded liability.
findings.matters: A structural deficit in schools funding that is unmet by government represents a contingent liability that erodes financial flexibility and requires ongoing borrowing to cover. This is particularly acute for lenders assessing whether the council can service its debts when mandatory spend on schools is outpacing funding.
findings.figures: £20.000 million on 31 March 2026 and increasing by approximately another £8.000 million during 2026/27
findings.quote: Pressures on school funding, particularly on the High Needs Block has resulted in a deficit on the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG). This is anticipated to be £20.000 million on the 31 March 2026 and increasing by approximately another £8.000 million during 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 10.2 Appendix 2 - Assurances from Director of Finance - Signed PW
findings.headline: Budget gap projected for 2026/27 after exhausting £20+ million in savings over four years
findings.detail: The council has delivered 'over £20 million' in savings in the last four financial years and 'even more over the past decade', yet the Medium-Term Financial Strategy now 'projecting a budget gap for 2026/27'. The CFO acknowledges 'limited scope for further savings' because of 'stretching both frontline and back-office services', indicating the council has reached the limit of what can be cut.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether budget pressures are cyclical (fixable through efficiency) or structural (requiring external intervention). Exhausted savings capacity and a persistent gap indicate a structural funding problem with no near-term internal solution.
findings.figures: £20 million+ savings over 4 years; projected gap for 2026/27; no identified savings solution
findings.quote: Despite the best efforts of the Authority, delivering significant levels of savings over the last four financial years (over £20 million) and even more over the past decade, the persistence and scale of pressures, particularly in high-cost children's care placements, combined with years of reducing resourcing levels through the outdated funding formula, reserves are now at a critically low level.

findings.paper_title: 10.2 Appendix 2 - Assurances from Director of Finance - Signed PW
findings.headline: Application for £15 million emergency government borrowing to cover 2026/27 budget gap
findings.detail: Unable to identify savings to balance the 2026/27 budget, the council has applied for £15 million under a government scheme that allows councils to 'capitalise revenue pressures for the coming year and fund them through borrowing, repayable over an extended period'. The CFO describes this as 'a vital bridge' to stability, but it is in essence borrowing to cover operational deficits.
findings.matters: A lender must understand the council is planning to borrow to mask structural spending problems rather than balance operationally. This indicates the underlying financial position is unsustainable and borrowing is delaying, not solving, the core issue.
findings.figures: £15 million provisional application amount
findings.quote: the Authority has made an application to the Government's scheme that allows additional financial flexibilities, allowing councils to capitalise revenue pressures for the coming year and fund them through borrowing, repayable over an extended period. For Redcar and Cleveland, it would provide a vital bridge to the more stable financial position forecast within the current MTFS period. An initial assessment of the projected budget gap for 2026/27 has informed a provisional application amount of £15 million.

findings.paper_title: 10.2 Appendix 2 - Assurances from Director of Finance - Signed PW
findings.headline: £5.075 million revenue overspend in 2024/25 with £2.9 million overspend forecast for 2025/26
findings.detail: The council significantly overshot its budget, despite mitigation measures that reduced the Q1 2024/25 overspend forecast from £12.369 million. The 2025/26 position remains unbalanced, with the CFO noting the council is 'exposed to high demand pressures in children's social care which make this position more challenging'. In-year measures from 2024/25 remain in place but have not closed the gap.
findings.matters: Persistent overspending signals the council cannot live within budget and is relying on reserves to balance. This pattern raises whether future budget forecasts are realistic and suggests the underlying problem is structural, not temporary.
findings.figures: £5.075m final overspend 2024/25; £12.369m Q1 forecast; £2.9m Q2 2025/26 forecast
findings.quote: The Council did however report throughout the year on significant financial pressures in the revenue budget, particularly in relation to Children's Social Care, pay award and home-to-school transport which resulted in an eventual overspend at year end of £5.075 million.

findings.paper_title: 10.2 Appendix 2 - Assurances from Director of Finance - Signed PW
findings.headline: Reserves depleted to critically low level of £18.782 million from £42.717 million in March 2021
findings.detail: The council's general reserves have fallen sharply over four years. The CFO warns of 'the risk of reserves being depleted to an unacceptably low level' and states reserves must now 'absorb the eventual aggregate overspend position likely in 2025/26'. At the current trajectory, the council has limited buffer to absorb any service demand shock.
findings.matters: A lender assessing risk needs to know the council's financial resilience. Critically low reserves indicate limited capacity to weather unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls, raising default risk significantly.

findings.paper_title: RTPHA 26-27 Revenue Budget Dec 2025 final

However, delivery of this objective is now explicitly conditional on how the trade deal is implemented. The 2026/27 budget shows a £207k surplus before member council contributions, but this is contingent on POAO income continuing at 2025/26 levels.

The draft 26/27 budget implies a surplus before Riparian contributions. The delivery of this objective continue to be closely assessed as the new EU Trade Deal is implemented.

findings.paper_title: RTPHA 26-27 Revenue Budget Dec 2025 final
findings.headline: Authority plans £175k reserve distribution in 2025/26 specifically to absorb anticipated trade deal impact

For 2025/26, the council is estimating a £0.278m net deficit after accounting for projected property growth; without the growth benefit (£0.738m), the underlying deficit would be worse.

The prior-year increase was driven by growth in discounts, exemptions and council tax support combined with higher-than-estimated bad debt provisions.

This £3.406m total must be factored into the 2026/27 budget. The deficit arose from worsening 2024/25 outturn and a reduction in liability due to reprofiling of growth on Teesworks.

findings.detail: The council faces sustained demographic and cost pressures in children's services. The number of children in care has increased with higher complexity requiring more expensive residential and supported accommodation placements, compounded by market insufficiency. The council has modelled demand and set aside a growth allocation to contain increases within £4m per annum from 2026/27 onwards. Additional £3m capital investment is planned over two years for in-borough accommodation development.
findings.matters: Persistent high-cost children's social care demand is a core driver of the council's financial distress and budget gap. This is not a transitory pressure; the council projects £4m annual growth indefinitely, suggesting structural service cost increases.

findings.detail: The council is applying for participation in the government's Additional Financial Flexibilities scheme, which allows councils to capitalise revenue pressures and fund them through borrowing repayable over extended periods. An initial budget gap assessment has informed a provisional application of £15m. The scheme requires external assurance from MHCLG with review in early January and final approval anticipated in February. The council states this is a bridge to a more sustainable position forecast within the MTFS period.
findings.matters: Dependency on a government exceptional finance scheme signals acute financial distress and indicates the council cannot balance its budget through normal income and savings. Scheme approval is not yet confirmed and timeline aligns with budget-setting, creating implementation risk.

The MTFS reserve is forecast to reach only £6.063m at the end of 2026/27.

findings.headline: Imminent coastal erosion at Cowbar Lane and climate event impacts create unbudgeted capital and resilience risks
findings.detail: The council faces imminent coastal erosion risk at Cowbar Lane with direct financial mitigation costs and legal/reputational exposure. Separately, extreme weather events (flooding, storms, heatwaves) are increasing with limited council resources to recover, creating a financial impact on the ability to deliver critical statutory services.
findings.matters: Both ongoing and imminent capital liabilities in a council already identifying tight financial constraints raises questions about borrowing headroom and service resilience.
findings.figures: Coastal erosion rated Major/Almost Certain (20) both initially and residually; climate change rated Major/Almost Certain (20) initially, residually Major/Likely (16)
findings.quote: There is a financial impact with this risk, with limited council resources to recover from extreme events, as well as the impact on our day-to-day ability to deliver our critical and statutory services.

findings.paper_title: 8.1 Corporate Risk Register - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Children's social care placement costs are the main driver of medium-term financial plan pressures, with inadequate local provision to meet demand
findings.detail: The council identifies increased placements costs for children in care as the primary financial pressure forcing the need for significant savings. Simultaneously, the council notes a shortage of adequate and suitable placements locally or regionally, creating a risk that rising demand cannot be met through regulated provision, threatening the council's ability to fulfil statutory safeguarding duties.
findings.matters: Unfunded statutory obligations that cannot be solved through efficiency or market provision create direct financial and legal risk; lenders need to understand whether savings targets account for demand that cannot be constrained.
findings.figures: RG02 and CF38 both initially Catastrophic/Almost Certain (25), residually Major/Likely (16)
findings.quote: The main driver of the financial pressures is increased placements costs for children needing to come into care due to increased demand and complexity of need and market insufficiency.

findings.paper_title: 8.2 Member Report Corporate Risk Register November 2025 - Appendix 2
findings.headline: Very low reserves creating vulnerability to unexpected pressures in a critical two-year financial period
findings.detail: The council's budget report explicitly identified that the next two years represent a critical period requiring extra vigilance due to very low levels of reserves. These reserves provide minimal buffer against demand and cost pressures, particularly given the volatility in children's services and statutory demand.
findings.matters: Reserves are the only buffer a council has when demand pressures exceed budget. Very low reserves combined with high-volatility statutory services means the council has limited ability to absorb unexpected cost increases without emergency action or further budget cuts.
findings.figures: No specific reserve figures in this document, but noted as 'very low levels'
findings.quote: The budget report highlighted that the next two years is a critical period where the Council must be extra vigilant regarding its financial position, recognising the very low levels of reserves the Council has, the risks it faces with statutory services encountering demand and cost pressures

findings.paper_title: 8.2 Member Report Corporate Risk Register November 2025 - Appendix 2
findings.headline: Children in care numbers remain elevated and volatile (currently 420), with transformation plan required to reduce costs
findings.detail: Numbers of children in care peaked at approximately 440 between December 2023 and June 2024, have reduced to 400 but now stand at 420. The document notes this situation is volatile and can shift immediately with large sibling groups or children moving into area with specialist needs. A transformation plan is in place to reduce demand and costs through prevention, early intervention, and regional partnerships.
findings.matters: This is the direct driver of the £2.674 million overspend. Placement costs for children in care are among the most expensive statutory services the council delivers. Volatility and the reliance on unproven transformation initiatives to control costs creates material budget risk.
findings.figures: Peak of approximately 440 children (Dec 2023–June 2024); currently 420 children; target is to reduce through transformation plan
findings.quote: The numbers of children in our care significantly increased from Dec 2023 to June 2024 at approximately 440 children. This has reduced to a level of 400 but currently stands at 420. This is a positive picture however as set out above the situation can be volatile and a large sibling group coming into our care can increase numbers immediately.

findings.paper_title: 8.2 Member Report Corporate Risk Register November 2025 - Appendix 2
findings.headline: Fair Funding Reform will deliver less benefit than hoped and phased over three years, delaying financial relief
findings.detail: The council expected Fair Funding Reform announced in June 2025 to provide significant additional funding to reflect deprivation and cost pressures. Initial analysis shows the council will benefit, but not as much as anticipated. Critically, any increase in funding will be phased in over three years, extending the period before the council receives full allocation.
findings.matters: This is a material income shortfall against expectations that the council was relying on to ease medium-term budget pressures. The phased implementation means financial relief is delayed, forcing the council to rely on savings delivery and contingencies for longer.
findings.figures: Fair Funding phased in over 3 years; Budget delayed to late November 2025, Provisional Local Government Financial settlement expected before Christmas 2025
findings.quote: The initial analysis of the reforms is that RCBC do stand to benefit, but not by as much as we had hoped. The increase in funding is currently expected to be phased in over 3 years increasing the time frame before the Authority receives the full allocation following Fair Funding.

findings.paper_title: 8.2 Member Report Corporate Risk Register November 2025 - Appendix 2
findings.headline: £2.674 million overspend projected for 2025/26, primarily driven by children's social care placement costs
findings.detail: The council is forecasting an overspend of £2.674 million for the current year, down from £6.468 million at the same point last year. However, this remains a significant concern given the council's very low reserves. The overspend is primarily driven by increased pressures within Children's Services, particularly the growing demand for expensive placement types and escalation of needs following placement disruptions.
findings.matters: An overspend of this magnitude against very low reserves indicates the council is consuming reserves at a time when it has minimal buffer for further pressures. This directly affects creditworthiness and the council's ability to weather unexpected shocks.
findings.figures: £2.674 million projected overspend for 2025/26; £6.468 million projected overspend at same point last year
findings.quote: The initial forecast for this financial year indicates a projected overspend of £2.674 million, which represents an improvement compared to the £6.468 million projected overspend at this point last year. However, it remains a significant concern, particularly in the context of ever-decreasing reserves.

findings.paper_title: 8. Member Report Corporate Risk Register November 2025
findings.headline: Coastal erosion at Cowbar Lane escalated to corporate red risk requiring immediate action on phase 1 of 10-year plan
findings.detail: Following recent rockfall and landslip at Cowbar Lane, the council has escalated coastal erosion back to red-rated corporate risk status after previously downgrading it to directorate level. The risk includes impacts to residents, property, and the highway, plus financial costs to mitigate and potential legal challenges. Phase 1 of a 10-year coastal strategy now requires urgent implementation.
findings.matters: Lenders need visibility of urgent capital commitments and infrastructure risks that could create unbudgeted costs or legal liabilities from failing to address coastal hazards.
findings.figures: No specific cost for phase 1 provided; 10, 25 and 50-year coastal plans in place
findings.quote: phase 1 of the 10-year plan, now needs actioning as soon as possible due to the imminent risk to the highway, which is why it has been escalated again to a corporate red risk for further review and monitoring

findings.paper_title: 6.6 Annex 1 - RCBC internal audit progress report November 2025
findings.headline: Planning delivery is constrained by outdated Local Plan and unresourced enforcement backlog
findings.detail: The planning applications audit found the council has an outdated Local Plan and a significant backlog of planning enforcement cases with no structured performance reporting. A temporary enforcement officer has been appointed to clear the backlog, with a permanent officer to be appointed within six months. A resilience review is underway to prevent future backlogs.
findings.matters: A planning backlog and outdated Local Plan can constrain the pace of economic development and capital scheme delivery, and extended enforcement delays may allow non-compliance issues to accumulate.
findings.figures: Permanent officer appointment deadline: within six months of October 2025 (approximately April 2026)
findings.quote: There is a backlog of planning enforcement cases and no structured performance reporting against policy targets.

findings.paper_title: 6.6 Annex 1 - RCBC internal audit progress report November 2025
findings.headline: Mandatory training for highways staff has expired, creating a critical control gap
findings.detail: The highways asset management audit identified that training records show mandatory training for multiple highways staff has expired. Management actions to update the staff training matrix and introduce a process to monitor current and future training needs are due 31 December 2025. This is flagged as a critical priority finding.
findings.matters: Expired mandatory training in highways creates operational and safety risks, and the fact it has gone unaddressed suggests management is not adequately monitoring compliance with essential training requirements.
findings.figures: Deadline to bring training records up to date: 31 December 2025
findings.quote: Training records for staff indicate that mandatory training for multiple highways staff has expired.

findings.paper_title: 6.6 Annex 1 - RCBC internal audit progress report November 2025
findings.headline: Multiple audit actions remain overdue, including three critical actions from 2025
findings.detail: Of 62 actions followed up as of 31 October 2025, 12 remain overdue. Three critical actions and two significant actions from a CCTV audit were originally due 31 March 2025, revised to 30 September 2025, and remain incomplete. Two further significant actions for school business continuity and IT disaster recovery have been outstanding since 31 December 2024. This pattern indicates implementation capacity or prioritization issues.
findings.matters: Persistent failure to implement agreed audit remedial actions suggests control weaknesses are not being addressed, exposing the council to ongoing risk from known control gaps.
findings.figures: 12 actions overdue; 3 critical and 2 significant actions from CCTV audit originally due March 2025; 2 significant actions outstanding since December 2024
findings.quote: At the time of reporting, twelve actions are overdue. The three critical actions and two of the significant actions relate to an audit of CCTV. These actions were originally due by 31st March 2025 and this was revised to 30th September 2025. They still remain outstanding

findings.paper_title: 6.6 Annex 1 - RCBC internal audit progress report November 2025
findings.headline: Statutory flood risk documents remain uncontrolled and critical actions are overdue
findings.detail: The audit found the council has failed to maintain several statutory documents required by the Flood and Water Management Act 2010 and Flood Risk Regulations 2009. A specialist consultant is being appointed to update them, with critical actions due 30 November 2025 and March 2026. The council also lacks an up-to-date flood risk asset register as required by statute, and gully maintenance is under-resourced and reactive.
findings.matters: Statutory non-compliance on flood risk management exposes the council to legal liability and potential enforcement action from DEFRA or the Environment Agency, and suggests governance weaknesses in how critical compliance obligations are managed.
findings.figures: Multiple critical and significant actions due by 30 November 2025, 31 March 2026, and 30 April 2026
findings.quote: The Council has failed to maintain several statutory and strategic flood risk management documents in accordance with the Flood and Water Management Act 2010 (FWMA 2010), the Flood Risk Regulations 2009, and national policy frameworks
